reelection.rule: Rule: end of the current class term in legislators-current.yaml. Class 3 ends 2029-01-03. The November before that January 3 end is November 2028. The file does not store the election day, so no day of the month is shown.

vote_frequency.label: In this cached set only (the latest 40 Senate votes, not a lifetime record): 40 of 40. Yea or Aye: 30. Nay or No: 10. Not Voting: 0. Of 40 Yea or Nay votes where the Republican majority could be computed, 39 (98%) matched that majority (majority = the side most of that party's members voting Yea or Nay took; on average 51 members of that party voted Yea or Nay per roll call).

finance.disclosure_note: Disclosed contributions only; donors behind groups that do not report their own donors are not in this feed.
finance.cycle_rule: Senate filings use the two-year cycle of the next election. the current term ends 2029-01-03, so the preceding November election is 2028.
finance.scope_note: Figures are committee receipts and itemized Schedule A for this two-year cycle only. This is not career fundraising. Schedule E outside spending is not included.

stands_for.caption: Grouped by Congress.gov's official policy area. Shows how they voted, not why. Final-passage, amendment, and procedural votes can mean different things; read the note for each.
stands_for.scope: Senate votes 1–262 of the 119th Congress, session 2 (262 votes, January 5, 2026 to November 12, 2026), from the Senate LIS.
stands_for.majority_rule: Party majority = the Yea/Nay side taken by most members of that party who voted Yea or Nay on that roll call, counted from the party code in the roll-call XML (all members, including ones no longer serving). Ties have no majority.
stands_for.factual_flag: Not yet summarized: this line is built only from the official vote question and the bill's official title.

said_voted.caption: Posts are shown as written. A post is matched to a vote only when it names the bill number or the bill's official title. A post can mention a bill for many reasons.
said_voted.topic_caption: Recent posts grouped by simple keyword rules that are identical for every member (published at /x_topic_rules.json). A post listed under a topic is not claimed to be about any specific vote; a post can appear under more than one topic.

posts.text: I warned: “In coming years, the pace of technological innovation and deployment will only quicken. The new administration will need a systematic and sustained approach.” Two years later, it is even more critical to have a tech strategy for countering China. Read my full essay

Two years ago, I laid out a “Tech Power Playbook” for U.S. domestic prosperity and economic and national security. It focused on maintaining American dominance in critical and emerging technologies.
https://t.co/VIpE4QsLdw

Congrats to @IndianaUniv on the opening of its Applied Research Center (ARC) facility in Bloomington. 
The ARC is a new university-wide platform that will accelerate partnerships in critical fields like microelectronics, cybersecurity, AI, and biotech. Focused on national security, ARC will be a foundry of ideas that keeps America prepared for whatever lies over the horizon.
Great day in Bloomington to see another championship team. Congrats to IU men’s soccer on winning the Big Ten tourney! https://t.co/vekS9vlhkA

Great to see more than $1.6 billion for the new Indianapolis VA facility included in this year’s proposed VA funding bill. This funding will support construction of a state-of-the-art facility to better serve Hoosier veterans. 

This project is important for veterans across Indiana, and I’ll continue pushing to ensure this funding remains in the final package.

Everyone has different financial circumstances, and this effort will empower workers to direct employer contributions where they need them most.

Thank you to America’s veterans and their families for your dedication to protecting our freedoms. Today, we honor all the brave men and women who have served and sacrificed for our nation. https://t.co/y8taz2oxFz

America’s permitting system takes too long and costs too much. Permitting reform will cut red tape and lower energy costs for Hoosier families. Indiana is the most manufacturing intensive state in the nation, and fixing this broken system will fuel future growth. Congress needs to get this done.

For 251 years, the @USMC has kept us safe at sea, on land, and in the air.

Given the actions of China and other bad actors, tariffs can be a useful tool to bring countries to the negotiating table – but there needs to be a table, and a deal worth making.

Our combat-wounded veterans have sacrificed so much in service to our country, and they deserve the full benefits they have earned.

The Major Richard Star Act would ensure these veterans receive all the pay and benefits they deserve. Congress needs to get this legislation across the finish line.

https://t.co/AmPYWSRwEu

Following the election on Tuesday night, I’ve spent time talking with a variety of folks from across our state and will continue to do so. Hoosiers want what I want: government at every level intently focused on deliverables — honest governance, more economic opportunity, lower prices, and a safer country. These are simple priorities but essential to helping families and restoring trust. Let’s get back to work.

My team joined @ENERGY Assistant Secretary for Electricity Katie Jereza in Carmel today to highlight more than $1.8 million in investments to strengthen Indiana’s electric grid.

I want to congratulate Katie Bailey on recently being named Director of the White House Office of Legislative Affairs.

My team and I worked closely with Katie when she served as Legislative Director for @GovBraun during his time in the Senate. She is a true professional who will effectively advance the President’s agenda.

Katie also has a deep understanding of Indiana and the Midwest, which I am excited for her to bring to this role. I look forward to working with Katie and her team.
